facts.fact_text: The case concerns police ill-treatment of the applicants during a political rally on 6 May 2012 at Bolotnaya Square.

The background facts relating to the planning, conduct and dispersal of the assembly at Bolotnaya Square are set out in more detail in the judgment of Frumkin v. Russia (no. 74568/12, §§ 7-65, 5 January 2016).
Both applicants participated in the political rally on 6 May 2012.
The first applicant (Mr Zakharov) was one of the organisers of the political rally on 6 May 2012.
During the dispersal of the meeting on 6 May 2012, the police allegedly hit the first applicant (Mr Zakharov) on the head with a rubber truncheon.
During the dispersal of the meeting on 6 May 2012, the police allegedly hit the second applicant (Ms Varzhabetyan) on the head with a rubber truncheon.
Two photographs submitted by the first applicant (Mr Zakharov) show him at the site of the events at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012 with his face bleeding.
According to the first applicant (Mr Zakharov), having received a blow to the head, he lost consciousness.
The first applicant (Mr Zakharov) submitted a medical certificate dated 6 May 2012 stating that he had been diagnosed with a contused wound of the frontal lobe.
The second applicant (Ms Varzhabetyan) provided links to YouTube videos showing the clashes between the police and the protesters at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
The YouTube videos provided by the second applicant (Ms Varzhabetyan) indicate that she was surrounded by police officers when she fell and started screaming.

The YouTube videos provided by the second applicant (Ms Varzhabetyan) show other participants in the assembly carrying her and shouting at the police officers, accusing them of hitting an elderly woman, referring to the second applicant (Ms Varzhabetyan).
The medical certificate submitted by the second applicant (Ms Varzhabetyan) attested that she had sustained a head injury on 6 May 2012.
The medical certificate submitted by the second applicant (Ms Varzhabetyan) attested that she had soft tissue bruises on the right side of her head on 6 May 2012.
The medical certificate submitted by the second applicant (Ms Varzhabetyan) attested that she had soft tissue bruises in the perineal region on 6 May 2012.
A medical certificate dated 7 May 2012 stated that the second applicant (Ms Varzhabetyan) had had health problems as a result of the trauma she had experienced on 6 May 2012.
A medical certificate dated 8 June 2012 stated that the second applicant (Ms Varzhabetyan) had had health problems as a result of the trauma she had experienced on 6 May 2012.

Section 20 of the Police Act (no. 3 of 7 February 2011, as in force at the material time) provided that police officers might use physical force, including combat methods, to arrest individuals who had committed criminal or administrative offences.

Section 20 of the Police Act (no. 3 of 7 February 2011, as in force at the material time) provided that police officers might use physical force, including combat methods, to overcome resistance to lawful orders if non-violent methods did not ensure compliance with responsibilities entrusted to the police.
Section 21 of the Police Act (no. 3 of 7 February 2011) laid down an exhaustive list of circumstances in which special means, including rubber truncheons, might be used.
Section 21 of the Police Act (no. 3 of 7 February 2011) permitted rubber truncheons to be used to repel an attack on civilians or police officers.
Section 21 of the Police Act (no. 3 of 7 February 2011) permitted rubber truncheons to be used to overcome resistance shown to a police officer.

Section 21 of the Police Act (no. 3 of 7 February 2011) permitted rubber truncheons to be used to repress mass disorder and put an end to collective actions disrupting the operation of transport, means of communication and legal entities.
Section 21 of the Police Act (no. 3 of 7 February 2011) prohibited hitting a person on the head with a rubber truncheon.

Section 22 of the Police Act (no. 3 of 7 February 2011) stated that the use of special means to suppress an unlawful, but peaceful manifestation that did not disrupt the operation of transport, means of communication and legal entities was prohibited.
